subject: Art & Design
title: Bauhaus: Where Art Met Industry
description: Learn Bauhaus: Where Art Met Industry in one minute.

hook.text: In 1919, a German school tried to erase the line between fine art and practical design.

buildup.text: The Bauhaus combined painting, sculpture, architecture, and crafts into one curriculum.

discovery.text: Their principle: form follows function. If it works well, it will naturally look right.

twist.text: The Nazis shut it down in 1933. Its teachers fled to America and reshaped global design.

climax.text: Every minimalist chair, clean font, and glass building owes a debt to Bauhaus thinking.

punchline.text: The Nazis closed a school. Its ideas conquered the world.

quiz.question: What was the Bauhaus's core principle?

details.summary: The Bauhaus school (1919-1933) united fine art, craft, and industrial design under one roof in Weimar Germany. Teachers like Kandinsky, Klee, and Moholy-Nagy developed a curriculum that treated all design disciplines as interconnected. The Nazis closed it, scattering its ideas worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Bauhaus created the foundation of modern design education. Its principle that good design should be functional, accessible, and producible at scale shaped everything from furniture to typography to architecture throughout the 20th century.
takeaways: United fine art, craft, and industrial design under one curriculum
Kandinsky, Klee, and Moholy-Nagy were among its teachers
Nazi closure scattered Bauhaus ideas worldwide

faq.question: What made Bauhaus teaching different from traditional art schools?
faq.answer: Traditional schools separated fine art from applied craft. Bauhaus required all students to study both, starting with a foundational course in materials and form. Students then specialized in workshops — weaving, metalwork, ceramics, typography — blending artistic vision with technical skill.

faq.question: What Bauhaus designs do we still use today?
faq.answer: Marcel Breuer's tubular steel Wassily Chair, Marianne Brandt's tea infuser, Wilhelm Wagenfeld's table lamp, and Herbert Bayer's Universal typeface all originated at the Bauhaus. The school's design principles also underpin IKEA's mass-produced functional aesthetic.
